title: Systems of differential equations
objectives: Read stability and the half-life from the eigenvalues.
Compute the matrix exponential in NumPy through the eigenvalues.

screens.title: Two spreads that pull on each other
screens.prose: Two spreads pull on each other: $u_1' = -2u_1 + u_2$ and $u_2' = u_1 - 2u_2$. At $t = 0$ we have $u_1 = 1$ and $u_2 = 0$. Slide time forward and watch both.
screens.question: Where do the two spreads head?

options.text: Both die away to 0, with $u_2$ rising first

options.why: You split the starting total, 1, evenly. The caption shows both falling well below 0.5.
$u_2$ does rise at first, but the $-2u_2$ term wins once $u_2$ is large enough. Slide past $t = 1$.
Neither curve crosses 0 or turns back up. Each rise or fall is smooth.

feedback.correct: Both spreads decay to 0. $u_2$ rises to about 0.19 near $t = 0.55$ before falling.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Slide $t$ from 0 to 5 and read both values in the caption.

explain.text: Both spreads shrink to 0, and $u_2$ peaks early because $u_1$ feeds it. What we want is a formula for $\mathbf{u}(t)$. The matrix form $\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ with $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} -2 & 1 \\ 1 & -2 \end{pmatrix}$ will give it.

screens.title: Along an eigenvector the system decouples
screens.prose: In matrix form the system is $\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$. Try the eigenvector matrix $\mathbf{X}$, with columns $(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$. Multiply $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$ and read what each column is.
screens.question: Fill in $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{X}$.

hints.text: Row 1 of $\mathbf{A}$ is $(-2, 1)$ and row 2 is $(1, -2)$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Multiply $\mathbf{A}$ by each column of $\mathbf{X}$ in turn.

explain.text: $\mathbf{A}$ sends $(1, 1)$ to $-1(1, 1)$ and $(1, -1)$ to $-3(1, -1)$, so the eigenvalues are $-1$ and $-3$. Along $(1, 1)$ the system is just $u' = -u$, and along $(1, -1)$ it is $u' = -3u$. Each one-variable equation is solved by $e^{\lambda t}$.

screens.title: Split the start into eigenvectors
screens.prose: The start $\mathbf{u}_0 = (1, 0)$ is a mix of the two eigenvectors: $\mathbf{u}_0 = c_1(1, 1) + c_2(1, -1)$. Each part then follows its own equation, $c_i(t) = c_i e^{\lambda_i t}$.
screens.question: Find $c_1$ and $c_2$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Solve $c_1 + c_2 = 1$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 0$.

byKey.r0c1: The two rows give $c_1 + c_2 = 1$ and $c_1 - c_2 = 0$. Adding them gives $2c_1 = 1$.
byKey.r1c1: $c_1 = c_2$ from row 2, and $c_1 + c_2 = 1$ from row 1.

explain.text: $\mathbf{c} = \mathbf{X}^{-1}\mathbf{u}_0 = (\tfrac12, \tfrac12)$. The solution is $\mathbf{u}(t) = \tfrac12e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ 1 \end{pmatrix} + \tfrac12e^{-3t}\begin{pmatrix} 1 \\ -1 \end{pmatrix}$. At $t = 0$ it returns $(1, 0)$.

hints.text: $u_1$ is the first entry of both parts.
The first entry of each eigenvector is 1, so $u_1(t) = \tfrac12e^{-t} + \tfrac12e^{-3t}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the two parts, each with its factor $\tfrac12$.

byKey.diag: $e^{-2} = 0.1353$ uses the diagonal entry of $\mathbf{A}$ as the rate. The rates are the eigenvalues, $-1$ and $-3$.
byKey.nohalf: You left out the factor $\tfrac12$ on each part.
byKey.slow: $e^{-1}$ is the slow part alone, without the $\tfrac12$ and without the fast part.

explain.text: $u_1(1) = \tfrac12(0.3679 + 0.0498) = 0.2088$ and $u_2(1) = \tfrac12(0.3679 - 0.0498) = 0.1590$. That is $e^{\mathbf{A}}\mathbf{u}_0$, the first column of $e^{\mathbf{A}}$.

screens.prose: The two spreads always add to $u_1 + u_2 = e^{-t}$, because the fast parts cancel. Stability needs every eigenvalue to have a negative real part. The slowest one sets how long the system lingers.
screens.question: After how long has $u_1 + u_2$ halved?

hints.text: $t = \ln 2 = 0.693$. The decay rate is the eigenvalue $-1$.

byKey.fast: $\ln 2 / 3$ uses the fast eigenvalue. The fast part dies quickly, so the slow one sets the half-life.
byKey.diag: $\ln 2 / 2$ uses the diagonal entry $-2$ of $\mathbf{A}$, which is not an eigenvalue.
byKey.one: $t = 1$ is where $e^{-t}$ is $0.37$, past a half.

explain.text: The half-life is $\ln 2 / |\lambda_{\text{slow}}| = 0.693$. Every solution decays when every eigenvalue has a negative real part, and the one closest to 0 sets the pace.

screens.title: The slow mode sets the pace

screens.prose: Now $\mathbf{A} = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & -1 \\ 1 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$, the 90 degree rotation from the last lesson, with eigenvalues $\pm i$. Start from $\mathbf{u}_0 = (1, 0)$.
screens.question: What does the solution do?

options.text: It circles the origin for ever, at constant distance
It spirals in to the origin
options.why: Decay needs a negative real part. $\pm i$ has real part 0, so nothing shrinks.
Growth needs a positive real part. Here the real part is 0.
$\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}_0 = (0, 1)$ is not zero, so the point moves.

hints.text: $\mathbf{A}(1, 0) = (0, 1)$: straight up, at right angles to the position.
A velocity always at right angles to the position moves you round a circle.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{u}(t) = (\cos t, \sin t)$: a circle, because $e^{it}$ has size 1.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Check the direction of $\mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ against $\mathbf{u}$.

explain.text: The solution is $(\cos t, \sin t)$, since $e^{\pm it}$ always has size 1. Real part 0 means neither decay nor growth. For stability the real parts must be strictly negative.

screens.title: Eigenvalues with no decay

screens.prose: A colleague computes $e^{\mathbf{A}}$ by applying $\exp$ to every entry of $\mathbf{A}$. We want the top right entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}}$, the true matrix exponential at $t = 1$.
screens.question: What is the top right entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}}$?

options.why: You took $\exp$ of the entry 1. That is not $e^{\mathbf{A}}$: the series mixes entries through $\mathbf{A}^2$, $\mathbf{A}^3$ and so on.
That is the slow part alone. The entry is half the difference of the slow and fast parts.
That is the fast part alone. It enters with a minus sign and a factor $\tfrac12$ next to the slow part.

feedback.correct: The true entry is $0.1590$; entrywise $\exp$ would give $2.7183$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use $\mathbf{X}e^{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$, not $\exp$ on entries.

byKey.entry: You exponentiated the entry. The result $2.7183$ would even grow, while every solution of this system decays.
byKey.slow: You kept only $e^{-1}$. Both modes contribute, with weights $\tfrac12$ and $-\tfrac12$.

explain.text: Entrywise $\exp$ gives $\begin{pmatrix} 0.1353 & 2.7183 \\ 2.7183 & 0.1353 \end{pmatrix}$, which blows up the off-diagonal. The true $e^{\mathbf{A}} = \tfrac12\begin{pmatrix} e^{-1} + e^{-3} & e^{-1} - e^{-3} \\ e^{-1} - e^{-3} & e^{-1} + e^{-3} \end{pmatrix}$ has diagonal $0.2088$ and off-diagonal $0.1590$. Only a diagonal matrix can be exponentiated entry by entry, and then only on the diagonal.

The bracket is diagonal, with entries $1 + \lambda_it + \tfrac{(\lambda_it)^2}{2!} + \cdots = e^{\lambda_it}$

Pull the common factors $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$ out of the sum before reading the diagonal.
Series, powers, pull out, read the diagonal, name the result.

explain.text: Differentiating the series term by term gives $\tfrac{d}{dt}e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathbf{A}e^{\mathbf{A}t}$, so $\mathbf{u}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{u}_0$ solves $\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ and starts at $\mathbf{u}_0$. For your example this is the formula you found by splitting into eigenvectors.

Build the exponential in NumPy

widget.solution:
import numpy as np

def expm_eig(A, t):
    """Return e^(At), assuming A is diagonalisable."""
    A = np.asarray(A, dtype=float)
    vals, X = np.linalg.eig(A)
    E = np.diag(np.exp(vals * t))
    return np.real(X @ E @ np.linalg.inv(X))
widget.how: Check runs 6 hidden tests, with entries rounded to 4 decimal places (tolerance 0.00005). The first run loads NumPy: 1 to 3 seconds. This function assumes A is diagonalisable. Real matrices with complex eigenvalues work: the imaginary parts cancel.

hints.text: $e^{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}t}$ is a diagonal matrix with $e^{\lambda_it}$ on its diagonal.
`np.diag(np.exp(vals * t))` builds it from the eigenvalue array.

feedback.generic: Some tests failed. Build the diagonal matrix of exponentials, then sandwich it between $\mathbf{X}$ and $\mathbf{X}^{-1}$.

byKey.error: Your code stopped with an error. Replace each `...` with an expression.

explain.text:
The exponential is a sandwich: the eigenvector matrix, the diagonal of $e^{\lambda t}$, then the inverse.

```python
E = np.diag(np.exp(vals * t))
return np.real(X @ E @ np.linalg.inv(X))
```

The solution map is the matrix exponential applied to the start. At $t = 0$ it returns $\mathbf{u}_0$, and for a stable $\mathbf{A}$ it tends to $\mathbf{0}$ as $t$ grows.


screens.title: A credit rating in continuous time
screens.prose: A loan is Good or Bad. Column $j$ of the generator $\mathbf{Q}$ holds the yearly rates out of state $j$, Good then Bad. Each column adds to 0. $\mathbf{P}(t) = e^{\mathbf{Q}t}$ is a Markov matrix for every $t$. $\mathbf{Q}$ has eigenvalues $0$ and $-0.4$.
screens.question: A loan is Good now. What is the chance it is Bad after 1 year?

hints.text: The eigenvector for 0 is $(3, 1)$, which is the steady state $(0.75, 0.25)$ after scaling. The one for $-0.4$ is $(1, -1)$.

feedback.correct: $\mathbf{P}(1)$ has top left entry $0.9176$, so Bad has chance $1 - 0.9176 = 0.0824$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Read the (Bad, Good) entry of $e^{\mathbf{Q}}$: $0.25(1 - e^{-0.4})$.

byKey.rate: 0.1 is the rate, not a chance over a year. The chance must allow for loans that recover.
byKey.noreturn: $1 - e^{-0.1} = 0.0952$ ignores recovery from Bad, which the 0.3 rate allows.
byKey.steady: 0.25 is the long-run chance, reached only as $t$ grows.

explain.text: The eigenvalue 0 gives a part that never moves, the steady state $(0.75, 0.25)$. The eigenvalue $-0.4$ sets the pace: half the distance to it is gone in $\ln 2 / 0.4 \approx 1.73$ years. $\mathbf{P}(1)$ is a yearly Markov matrix like lesson 3's, with eigenvalue $e^{-0.4} = 0.670$ in place of $0.85$.

ideas: Along an eigenvector the system $\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ decouples: each part moves as $e^{\lambda t}$.

$e^{\mathbf{A}t} = \mathbf{X}e^{\boldsymbol{\Lambda}t}\mathbf{X}^{-1}$, from the series for $e^x$ and $\mathbf{A}^k = \mathbf{X}\boldsymbol{\Lambda}^k\mathbf{X}^{-1}$. The solution is $\mathbf{u}(t) = e^{\mathbf{A}t}\mathbf{u}_0$.
Every solution decays when every eigenvalue has a negative real part. The slowest one sets the half-life, and an eigenvalue 0 gives a steady state.

formula.name: Matrix exponential
formula.note: Exponentiate the eigenvalues, never the entries.

quiz.prose: A system $\mathbf{u}' = \mathbf{A}\mathbf{u}$ has eigenvalues $0.2$ and $-3$, and a generic start.
quiz.question: What happens to the solution?

options.text: It grows, slowly, because one eigenvalue is positive
It decays, since the larger eigenvalue in size, $-3$, is negative
options.why: You went by the biggest eigenvalue in size. The $-3$ part dies fast, and the $e^{0.2t}$ part is what is left.

options.text: It settles at a nonzero constant
options.why: Only an eigenvalue exactly 0 gives a part that stays put.
Oscillation needs complex eigenvalues. These are real.

feedback.correct: The $e^{0.2t}$ part grows and the $e^{-3t}$ part vanishes.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each part moves as $e^{\lambda t}$ for its own $\lambda$.

explain.text: After a short time the $e^{-3t}$ part is negligible, and $e^{0.2t}$ keeps rising. One positive eigenvalue makes the system unstable.

options.why: You applied $\exp$ to the zero entries and got $e^0 = 1$. $e^{\mathbf{A}}$ of a diagonal matrix keeps its zeros.
$e^{\mathbf{A}}$ is not $\mathbf{A}$. The series $\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A} + \cdots$ changes the diagonal.
You swapped the eigenvalues. The first diagonal entry of $e^{\mathbf{A}}$ comes from $-1$.

feedback.correct: A diagonal matrix has $\mathbf{X} = \mathbf{I}$, so $e^{\mathbf{A}} = \mathrm{diag}(e^{-1}, e^{2})$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. For a diagonal matrix, exponentiate the diagonal entries and keep the zeros.

explain.text: The series $\mathbf{I} + \mathbf{A} + \tfrac{\mathbf{A}^2}{2!} + \cdots$ stays diagonal, with $1 + a + \tfrac{a^2}{2!} + \cdots = e^{a}$ down the diagonal. The zeros stay zero.
